Add at least 2 designs to compare

Pitch-Level Totals — sum of all blocks sharing a pitch group (parallel-spring assumption)

What this shows: For each non-empty pitch group, the tool sums Kx, Ky, and Kxy across all member blocks. This assumes blocks along a pitch deflect together on a rigid belt (parallel springs). The pitch K_max and α are derived from the summed matrix. Caveat: rib-and-belt coupling and adjacent-block interactions are not modelled. Treat the pitch totals as a first-order aggregate / trend estimate, typically within 10-15% of a proper pitch-level FEA. Symmetry-driven Kxy cancellation (mirror-image pairs) is captured correctly.

Reference Validation — Fig 16 Z-Block (Simple Block with No Features)

This tab anchors the current solver against Fig 16 of Okonieski et al. (2003) — the "simple block with no features" Z-shaped polygon, swept across NSD from 2 to 8 mm. Block coordinates: (−8, −10), (12, −10), (12, −5), (25, 5), (25, 10), (6, 10), (6, 5), (−8, −5). Parameters: E = 6.89 N/mm², ν = 0.49, draft = 0°, parallel-end, no sipes. Reference values are digitized from the SNum Kx Parallel-end curve (filled triangles in Fig 16b) and the SNum Kxy curve in Fig 16c — i.e. the paper's parallel-end series, which matches this solver's mode.
How to read this: "Δ vs SNum" is the percent difference between the current solver and the published SNum curve at each NSD. Kx and Kxy are swept over NSD = 2…8 mm. Mean absolute error across the sweep is shown in the summary line. This is a reconstruction-based check, not a reproduction of Goodyear's proprietary implementation — the SNum discretisation algorithm is not public, so absolute values may differ while trends and magnitudes match.
Controls: Left-drag rotates · Wheel zooms · Right-drag or Ctrl-drag pans · The modebar at the plot's top-right has zoom-in/out, box zoom, pan, reset, and save PNG. Top face is shifted radially from the footprint centroid using offset = NSD × tan(draft). Concave polygons are meshed via ear-clipping triangulation, so Z-shaped blocks render without stray faces. This view is visual only — it doesn't feed the solver.

Governing Equations

Parallel-End Displacement (Eq 1 — interior footprint region):

δ = FL³ / (12EI) + FL / (GA)

Free-End Displacement (Eq 2 — cantilever at footprint edge):

δ = FL³ / (3EI) + 6FL / (5GA)

Stiffness (Eq 3):

K = F / δ

Directional Stiffness (Eq 4):

Kβ = Kx·cos²β + Ky·sin²β + Kxy·sin(2β)

Principal Direction (Eq A8):

tan(2α) = 2Kxy / (Kx − Ky)

Shear Modulus:

G = E / (2(1 + ν))

Polygon Section Properties (Shoelace / Green's theorem) — all in mm units:

A (mm²) = ½ |Σ (xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)|
Ixx (mm⁴) = Σ (yᵢ² + yᵢyᵢ₊₁ + yᵢ₊₁²) × crossᵢ / 12 − A·cy²
Iyy (mm⁴) = Σ (xᵢ² + xᵢxᵢ₊₁ + xᵢ₊₁²) × crossᵢ / 12 − A·cx²

Physics Assumptions

1. Beam analogy: Tread blocks are modelled as short beams fixed at the base (bonded to belt/carcass) and loaded at the contact surface. This is the fundamental simplification — real blocks are 3D rubber bodies, not idealised beams.

2. Small deformation / linear elasticity: All deformations are assumed small and the rubber behaves linearly. In reality, rubber is hyperelastic and tread blocks can undergo large deformations, especially under severe cornering.

3. Static analysis: Dynamic effects are ignored. Even though block excitation in a rolling tyre is ~12 Hz at highway speed, the model treats the problem as quasi-static.

4. No slip: The contact surface is assumed to remain bonded to the road (no sliding). This is reasonable for the interior footprint region but breaks down at the footprint exit where slip occurs.

5. Material isotropy: The rubber compound is treated as isotropic with uniform E and ν. Real tread compounds may exhibit anisotropy and temperature-dependent properties.

6. Nearly incompressible: Rubber with ν ≈ 0.49 gives G ≈ E/3. The model uses exact G = E/(2(1+ν)) without the incompressibility simplification.

Geometry Assumptions

1. Sub-block decomposition: Sipes split the block into independent rectangular sub-blocks acting as springs in parallel. Each sub-block's stiffness is computed independently and summed. The paper confirms this approach (no parallel axis theorem transfer between sub-blocks).

2. Equivalent rectangle: Polygon-shaped blocks are converted to an equivalent rectangle with the same A, Ixx, and Iyy. This preserves bending and shear behaviour but loses coupling effects (Kxy = 0 for equivalent rectangles).

3. Uniform draft angle: In the simplified input, all edges share the same draft angle. Height-averaged section properties are computed using harmonic mean integration over the block height.

4. Full-width sipes only: Sipes are assumed to extend completely across the block, creating independent sub-blocks. Partial-width sipes, which leave the block structurally connected around sipe endpoints, are not modelled.

5. Sipe thickness: Sipes remove a strip of material equal to sipe_t (default 0.5 mm). This directly reduces sub-block dimensions and contact area.

Analytical Limitations

1. No 3D stress distribution: The beam model cannot capture stress concentrations at sipe tips, groove corners, or re-entrant angles. FEA is needed for these.

2. Configuration-blind for same net-to-gross: Designs with the same contact area but different spatial arrangements (e.g., sipes in different positions) may produce the same stiffness values. The paper acknowledges this limitation (Table 1: L15, L16, L25, L26 give identical SNum results).

3. Coupling stiffness (Kxy): Kxy is computed directly from the full bending-inertia tensor using the sign-correct stiffness matrix K_bend = (12E/L³)·[[Iyy, +Ixy], [+Ixy, Ixx]], whose inverse gives the bending compliance C_bend = (L³/12E·det)·[[Ixx, −Ixy], [−Ixy, Iyy]]. Shear compliance L/GA·𝐈 (or 6L/5GA free-end) adds in series, and K = (C_bend + C_shear)⁻¹. For symmetric cross-sections (Ixy = 0) this gives Kxy = 0 identically and reduces exactly to Eq 1/2 for Kx, Ky. For asymmetric blocks or angled sipes, Kxy has the same sign as Ixy, matching the paper's Eq 4 convention K_β = Kx·cos²β + Ky·sin²β + Kxy·sin(2β).

4. Tapered-beam integration: For a block with draft, the cross-section varies along height. Rather than averaging section properties and plugging into a uniform-beam formula, the tool integrates compliance slice-wise via Castigliano's theorem: C_bend_ij = (1/E)·∫w(z)·(I⁻¹)_ij(z) dz with moment-squared weight w(z) = (L/2 − z)² for parallel-end and (L − z)² for free-end. Shear contributes ∫ dz/(G·A(z)). For a constant section this reduces identically to the paper's Eq 1 / Eq 2; for a tapered section it captures the proper variation along height.

5. Tiebar accuracy: The SNum approach loses accuracy when tiebar depth exceeds ½ to ⅔ of the NSD. Use FEA for deep tiebars.

6. Draft-angle convention: The input polygon is treated as the contact surface (top of the block, z = NSD). Positive draft flares the sides outward going down, so the base is wider than the top — which matches typical tyre-mould geometry and makes the block stiffer as draft increases (wider base → larger height-averaged cross-section).

7. Implementation note: This tool implements the beam-mechanics framework described by Okonieski et al. (2003). Section properties (A, Ixx, Iyy, Ixy) are computed via Green's theorem on the polygon. The no-sipe path uses Castigliano slice integration over 40 slices. The sipe path uses layer/sub-block decomposition: sub-block stiffness matrices summed in parallel within each layer, layer compliance matrices summed in series along height. Sub-block decomposition follows the paper's published principle using Sutherland-Hodgman polygon clipping. This is a reconstruction of the beam-mechanics framework, not a port of Goodyear's proprietary SNum discretization; relative trends and sensitivities match the paper closely, absolute values may differ.

8. Bending vs shear diagnostic: The preview and comparison table report the percentage of total compliance coming from bending and shear in X and Y. These percentages are compliance shares, not force shares. A high shear percentage means the total stiffness is mainly controlled by the area-based shear term, so rotating same-area rectangles may produce only small Kx/Ky differences. A high bending percentage means the second moment of area controls more strongly, so orientation effects become larger. The Output tab also includes NSD × L/D dominance maps, which show where the block moves from shear-controlled to bending-controlled behavior.

9. Optional shape factor extension: The HTML tool optionally adds an advanced shape multiplier M_shape = clamp(Mc · Mq · Me · Md). Here Mc = 1 + α(C − 0.90) with C = 4πA/P², Mq = 1 + αq(Q − 1) with Q = A/Ahull, Me = 1 − αe·Eturn where Eturn is the turning-angle excess after removing nearly-collinear points, and Md = 1 + αd(D − Dref) where D is a length-weighted axis-alignment index of the outline. This is not part of the original Okonieski formulation. It is an engineering extension added to penalise concave, edge-heavy, irregular, and poorly axis-aligned outlines and to better match literature trends for same-area blocks.

Winkler Foundation Contact Model (v22 extension)

What it is: The Winkler (1867) foundation model treats the contact face of the tread block as a bed of independent compressive springs. Each area element dA at position (x,y) on the contact surface deflects by δz and exerts a normal pressure proportional to local deflection:

pz(x,y) = kz · δz(x,y)    where    kz = E / NSD   [N/mm³]

Global equilibrium: For a rigid belt (TBR, EI_c = 0), δz is uniform across the contact face. Integrating over net contact area A_net gives:

Fz = kz · δz · A_net   →   pz = Fz / A_net   (uniform)

This recovers the scalar preload correction used in v21 — so for rigid-carcass (TBR), the Winkler model is mathematically equivalent to the prior approach, but now computed per-sub-block rather than as a single average.

Flexible carcass (PCR): When EI_carcass > 0, the belt/carcass bends under load, causing a parabolic δz distribution across the footprint. A dimensionless parameter α_carc is derived from the ratio of block foundation stiffness to carcass bending stiffness:

α_carc ≈ kz · A_net · Lx² / (24 · EI_c)   (capped at 1.8)

The relative deflection field becomes δz(x,y) ∝ 1 + α_carc · r² where r is the normalised radial distance from the footprint centroid. This produces higher pressure at the footprint edges for α_carc > 0, consistent with the known edge-loading behaviour of PCR tires with flexible carcasses.

Stiffness correction: The local pz at each sub-block centroid is used to compute a sub-block-specific SC factor (shape correction), which is applied inside the layer integration loop. This replaces the v21 uniform scalar SC correction with a spatially distributed one — the first physically meaningful distinction between uniformly-loaded and edge-loaded blocks in the tool.

Diagnostics reported: Uniformity ratio (mean/max pz), Edge Index (fraction of load carried in outer 25% of footprint radius), and Centroid Shift (distance between geometric centroid and load centroid). For rigid carcass, all three should be ~1.0, ~0.25, and ~0 mm respectively. Deviations indicate non-uniform loading driven by sipe layout or carcass flexibility.

Honest scope note: This is a single-modulus Winkler spring-bed model applied to the tread block only. It does not model tyre belt/carcass mechanics from first principles — EI_carcass is a user-specified input. It does not capture tangential (friction-dependent) normal-tangential coupling, stick-slip transitions, or dynamic pressure variation during rolling. It is best interpreted as a physically-motivated pressure distribution that improves sub-block SC weighting, not as a contact mechanics solver.

Performance Parameters (v24 extension)

Module 1 — Radial Stiffness Kz (updated v25)

The block compressive (radial) stiffness uses the Gent-Lindley shape factor correction for bonded rubber columns:

S = A / (NSD × P)  [—]    E_eff = E × (1 + 2kS²)  [N/mm²]    Kz = E_eff × A / NSD  [N/mm]

Shore hardness → k coefficient (v25): The coefficient k is now compound-dependent, taken from Sheridan (1992) Table 8.1 in Gent's Engineering with Rubber. k = 0.93 (Shore 30) to 0.57 (Shore 70), default 0.64 (Shore 60). k accounts for strain-softening and imperfectly elastic behaviour of filled rubber in simple shear. For unfilled natural rubber, k ≈ 1.0 (Orfeo et al. 2023). Changing from Shore 40 to Shore 70 changes Kz by up to ±25%.

Bulk compressibility correction (v25): At very high shape factors (S > ~3), the apparent compression modulus approaches the bulk modulus Kb ≈ 1100 N/mm². The corrected modulus is:

E_eff_corrected = E_eff / (1 + E_eff / Kb)    Kb = 1100 N/mm²

For typical tread blocks (S = 0.3–1.5), this correction is less than 0.1% and can be ignored. The tool flags when E_eff_uncorr > 100 N/mm² (S > ~3).

1.2 — Bending-shear correction (Sheridan Eq. 8.5a) — NOT applied

Sheridan (1992) Eq. 8.5a gives a correction to the shear spring rate when bending is significant: K_s,corrected = K_s / (1 + t²/36rg²). This was considered for Tier 1 but is not applied to the Okonieski engine for the following reason:

The Sheridan formula was derived for a simplified model where shear is the only deformation mode, and the correction approximately accounts for bending that the simple model ignores. The Okonieski beam model already explicitly separates bending and shear compliances: C_total = C_bend + C_shear. Applying the Sheridan correction on top of the already-correct C_shear term would double-count the bending contribution. Worse, because the correction is direction-dependent (uses Iyy for X, Ixx for Y), it would artificially equalize Kx and Ky by inflating the shear compliance of the stiffer direction — collapsing a 3.66 N/mm directional difference to 0.28 N/mm for a typical 30×22 PCR block. This is physically wrong and contradicts both the Okonieski model and measured tyre behaviour.

1.3 — Compression-Shear Coupling Index CSI (v25)

Orfeo et al. (2023) showed experimentally and analytically that vertical load reduces lateral stiffness, and that blocks can become laterally unstable. The critical load is estimated using Haringx/Thomas theory (their Eq. 21), with bending and shear stiffnesses from Muhr's finite-deformation formulation (Orfeo Eq. 22, at λ=1):

E_c,bend = 3G × (1 + 2S²/3)    B = E_c,bend × I_min    R = G × A
Pcr = (π²B/h²) / (1 + π²B/(R·h²))    CSI = Fz / Pcr

CSI interpretation: <0.10 = negligible effect (Kx/Ky accurate); 0.10–0.30 = moderate (Kx/Ky overestimated ~5–15%); >0.30 = significant (consider FEA). The tool displays a colour-coded banner. Note: this is a first-order estimate — the full Haringx coupled model is more accurate but beyond the scope of this screening tool.

1.4 — E_eff and bulk modulus surfaced (v25)

Both E_eff (uncorrected) and E_eff (bulk corrected) are now displayed. The bulk correction factor = E_eff_corrected / E_eff_uncorr is also shown. For typical tread blocks this is ≈1.000; it deviates noticeably only for very squat blocks (S > 3).

1.5 — Preload compression diagnostic (display only)

The tool now reports the vertical compression implied by the selected preload and computed Kz: δz = Fz/Kz and εz = δz/NSD × 100. This is a diagnostic only and does not feed back into the main Kx, Ky, Kxy solver or the Winkler pressure normalisation.

Module 2 — Cornering Stiffness Cα

Derived from the Fiala brush model. For a single block of lateral stiffness Ky in contact over length Lc, the moment-arm integral gives:

Cα = Ky × Lc / 2  [N/rad]    = Ky × Lc / 114.6  [N/deg]

Physical derivation: at slip angle α [rad], the block tip displacement at position x along the contact is δy = α × x. Integrating the force distribution: Fy = ∫₀^Lc (Ky/Lc) × α × x dx = Ky × α × Lc/2. So Cα = dFy/dα = Ky × Lc/2. Normalised: Cα* = Cα/Fz [1/rad]. Source: Pacejka, Tyre and Vehicle Dynamics, 3rd ed. 2012, Ch. 3.

PCR confidence: ✓. TBR confidence: ⚠ — non-uniform contact pressure across the patch width increases the effective moment arm. Apply a correction factor of 1.2–1.5× for TBR.

Module 3 — Braking/Longitudinal Slip Stiffness CS

By symmetry of the brush model:

CS = Kx × Lc / 2  [N/rad]    (longitudinal slip stiffness, = dFx/dκ at κ→0)

Source: Fiala, E., VDI Zeitschrift, Vol. 96, 1954. TBR caveat: belt stiffness couples adjacent blocks and increases effective CS beyond this formula. Treat as a lower bound for TBR.

Module 4 — Wear Energy Index (WEI)

Based on Grosch's concept of abrasion energy proportional to frictional work. For a block under combined loads Fx, Fy:

δx = Fx/Kx   δy = Fy/Ky   W = Fx·δx + Fy·δy = Fx²/Kx + Fy²/Ky  [N·mm]

The combined compliance WEI = √(Cx² + Cy²) [mm/N] is a geometry-only wear proxy — lower WEI means less tip deflection per Newton of force, which correlates to less abrasion. Source: Grosch, K.A., Proc. Royal Society, 1963; Lupker et al., Tyre Science and Technology, Vol. 32, 2004.

Module 5 — Natural Frequency and NVH

The block's fundamental frequency (cantilever first mode approximation):

fn = (1/2π) × √(K/m)  [Hz]    where   K [N/m] = Kx × 1000  ,   m [kg] = ρ × A × NSD × 10⁻⁹

Vehicle speed at resonance: V = fn × pitch_length × 0.0036 [km/h]. When the tread block excitation frequency (V / pitch_length) matches fn, structural amplification occurs, contributing to pass-by noise. Source: Sakata et al., Tyre Science and Technology, Vol. 18, 1990. TBR caveat: at highway speed, belt resonances and road texture interaction dominate over block natural frequency.

Module 6 — Worn Stiffness Trajectory

The existing engine is looped over NSD fractions {100%, 85%, 70%, 55%, 40%, 25%} to compute stiffness across the wear life. Expected behaviour: shear-dominated (PCR) blocks show near-linear Kx/Ky drop with NSD. Bending-dominated (TBR) blocks show a cubic drop — stiffness halves well before NSD halves. Kz drops linearly since E_eff × A / NSD scales with NSD⁻¹ for constant A. Source: Okonieski et al. (2003), Section 4.

Unit consistency note

All computations use the SI-mm system: force in N, length in mm, stress in N/mm² = MPa, stiffness in N/mm, mass in kg, time in seconds. Rubber density converts from kg/m³ to kg/mm³ via × 10⁻⁹. Angles are in degrees for display but radians for all internal trigonometry and stiffness ratios.

Applicability by tyre type

Modules 1, 4, 6 are fully applicable to both PCR and TBR. Modules 2 and 3 (cornering and braking stiffness) are derived from the Fiala brush model which assumes uniform contact pressure and a flexible carcass — both are better approximations for PCR than TBR. For TBR, cornering stiffness should be treated as a lower bound and multiplied by an empirical correction factor (1.2–1.5×). Module 5 (NVH) is indicative for PCR but limited for TBR where belt-dominated resonances govern noise.
